<Rep. Stacey E. Plaskett>: Thank you very much to the ranking member and thank you to the committee for bringing up this matter. For over 15 years, Haiti HOPE/HELP programs have supported both US and Haitian textile industries by granting Haiti duty-free access for apparel and textile products.
Building strong business ties between two neighboring nations, this bill, the Haiti Economic Lift Program Extension Act, reauthorizes HOPE/HELP trade preference program for an additional three years through December of 2028.
The bill also restores eligibility for certain textiles which were initially eligible for duty-free treatment but became ineligible due to changes in the harmonized tariff schedule.
Now, I would of course like to thank Ranking Member Neil, Chairman Smith, as well as Dr. Murphy, and I especially want to thank my longtime friend and fellow Hoya, Haiti's ambassador to the United States, Lionel Deleur, and for all of their leadership in keeping the light of Haiti HOPE alive in the House of Representatives. And of course the committee's trade staff led by Alexandra Whitaker, Mr. Rueda, O'Donovan, and former US trade representative ambassador Katherine Thai who supported our work to reauthorize the program for many years.
We know that Haiti faces overlapping humanitarian, political, and economic crisis and needs both economic and political stability. The circumstances in Haiti require immediate action. We know that presently over 60% of the people of Haiti are living below poverty with over 25% of the population living in extreme poverty. There is a 37% youth unemployment rate occurring right now in Haiti. With lowering female literacy and lower school enrollment rates, as well as the crime that we all know about, the circumstance of the gang control makes finding skilled work very very difficult.
The apparel sector is of incredible importance to Haiti's economy and presently is the foundation for the country's economic development. And when we talk about economic development of Haiti, let's not forget Haiti's history and how it came about that they came into this economic straight that they are in. Many of us are aware and I want to bring to the committee's attention again that in 1825 for their freedom Haiti was exacted a debt. Initially 150 million in gold was required by Haiti to pay to France. That was gone went down to 90 million in gold. That's 560 million in today's dollars. It took 122 years for Haiti to pay off that amount. Paying for freedom. What would have happened if the United States had to pay Britain for its freedom?
It's estimated that between 21 billion and 115 billion in economic losses occurred because Haiti had to pay that amount to France for freedom. That is what has put Haiti into the ex dire economic strait that it is in today. And it is our support of Haiti as well as an economic benefit to the United States through its apparel that will help lift them. Given the cascading job losses and extreme security crisis, Haiti cannot afford to wait any longer for reauthorization of the vital program. Without reauthorization, certainly companies will increasingly shift production away from Haiti unless it is clear that HOPE/HELP will continue.
You know, Haiti is our strategic ally. It is one of the few countries in the hemisphere that still recognize Taiwan, and US support for the Haiti's apparel sector is mutually beneficial. Haitian apparel utilizes a great deal of American grown cotton, and when it is in place, plays an essential role in further shifting supply chains out of China and into the Western Hemisphere. It's my hope that this short-term extension of three years will preserve production and jobs in Haiti while providing a runway for Congress to further strengthen this program, assisting Haiti in diversifying its economy beyond textile production, which can often be a global race to the bottom on labor costs.
Thank you to my colleagues for supporting Haiti and its people. Thank you for supporting the Caribbean Hemisphere. And thank you to the staff who labored to make this short-term compromise possible. Thank you.
Stacey E. Plaskett.
